idiom_name: validate_for_*() member called at the use, verdict in std::optional / std::expected, one-shot via std::call_once
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the carriers but not the timing: keep the candidate constructible from raw input and give it a use-named member such as validate_for_publish() returning std::optional<Error> or, on C++23, std::expected<void, Error>, then call it in the operation before the effect - std::optional and std::expected make a dedicated Validated<T> wrapper unnecessary. When the check is expensive and the aggregate is immutable afterwards, std::call_once with a std::once_flag memoises it for all threads, and std::optional is also the natural carrier for the incomplete fields themselves. A validator class hierarchy is still justified when rules are shared across types and composed at runtime; otherwise the member function is the smaller form.
pitfalls: Reading the value out of a disengaged std::optional is undefined behaviour and std::expected::value() throws bad_expected_access, so a verdict type that mixes 'not checked yet' with 'checked, no error' is a real bug source.

std::call_once does not cache exceptions: a validation that throws leaves the flag unset so the next caller retries, while a successful call caches the verdict forever - a later mutation therefore leaves a stale valid result unless a version counter is checked too.

A validator that keeps references or iterators into the candidate dangles when the candidate is mutated before the deferred call; validate a snapshot or make the candidate immutable for the lifetime of the verdict.
